#4593. How to Motivate Children for Success in School

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Parents in America and around the world agree on this: We want our children to succeed in school. Intense pressure for academic achievement now dominates the lives of many American families.

American students, however, are not doing well. Perhaps even more concerning, they seem to have less interest in learning. High school and college teachers across the country now assign less reading to their students, and students still complain that this is more than they can manage. Many American high school and college students no longer read books!

There are several possible causes for our children's loss of interest in learning, and different causes for different children. The impact of screens is certainly important. Children no longer have the attention span for reading. Instead, they are scrolling and watching short videos. They may even believe that, in this way, they are learning.

1. Express enthusiastic interest in your child’s interests, even if these are not the interests you would choose. Learning begins with interest. Children's instinctive interest and curiosity about the world are the starting point for their motivation and enjoyment of learning. As soon as children begin to talk, they are constantly asking questions, seeking information, and wanting to know “why.” Too often, in our understandable effort to help improve their skills, we neglect this essential aspect of children’s motivation.

Make note of moments of interest and talk with your children about what interests them. Ask questions. Do "research" together. Help them develop their interests into projects and goals.

The promise of rewards or the threat of punishment may lead to some short-term improvement in a child’s effort. But rewards and punishments cannot create interest, enjoyment, or long-term goals

2. Find the source of their anxiety, frustration, and discouragement. Parents often ask, "Why doesn’t he put more effort into his schoolwork? Why doesn’t he care?” The answer to these questions is almost always, “Because he is discouraged.”

Children may mask their discouragement with defiant or rebellious attitudes, and they may pretend that they don’t care. But they do care. If we look hard enough, we will find in every child some interest and a desire to do well.

Undiagnosed attention and learning disorders are a common source of discouragement and lack of sustained effort in children and adolescents. It is essential for parents and teachers to understand the impact of these difficulties. Even mild or moderate learning problems can be a source of anxiety, frustration, and low self-esteem.

3. Make note of every improvement, not every mistake. To solve the problem of discouragement, children need more encouragement and less criticism. Of course, to improve their skills, children need criticism. But they need encouragement even more. Encouragement is not false praise. We all need encouragement, even as adults, with every new challenge and skill we attempt to master.

4. Help them cultivate a growth mindset. Praise effort, not intelligence or talent. Praise learning, not grades. Then, on this foundation, we can set high standards and challenge children to work harder. But we will have to do this less often, because they will more often challenge themselves.

5. Appreciate their strengths. Students who seem unmotivated are often focused on their weaknesses, not on their strengths.

When I talk with “unmotivated” children, I often find qualities of intelligence, creativity, effort, and character that their parents and teachers have overlooked and that they may also fail to appreciate. When I point out these qualities, many children and adolescents feel deeply understood. For some, this is a transformative moment. Years later, these affirming statements are what they remember and value most about our work.

6. Make learning meaningful. Individual achievement alone—getting good grades in school—is a fragile source of motivation and effort, with a high cost in anxiety and stress. If we define achievement, however, as making a contribution to our families, our communities, our country, and the world, we offer children a much better goal and standard for success. We should help them become involved in projects that help their community, and we should be involved with them.

7. Have conversations. Every moment of dialogue with our children and grandchildren adds meaning and relevance to learning. Talk with your children about what they are studying—about civics and history, science, literature, and religion—and the importance of these subjects to our current lives. Talk with them about how others help us, about the good work that many people are doing, and what they can do to help others.

Conversation is a (partial) antidote to the addictive pull of screens. Before you ask, “Have you done your homework?” ask them about what they have been learning in school.

8. Establish "library hours" in your home. Even when children are highly motivated to do well in school, they still need to establish good work habits. They need to put away their devices, do their homework, and get enough sleep.

I encourage parents to set aside a specified time, early in the evening, as a homework or “library” hour. During the library hour, all electronics should be turned off (except for computers or tablets children need for schoolwork) for the entire family. No television, no video games, no phones.

Homework should be done in a communal place (as in a library), at the kitchen or dining room table. Especially with younger children, parents are present and available to help, offer encouragement, and answer questions. Then, when homework is done, there is time for play.

Most families have found these guidelines helpful for students of all ages. The result is an important lesson in self-discipline, fewer family arguments, and more success in school.

West, M. R. Student Test Scores Keep Falling. What's Really to Blame? Education Week, September 9, 2025.

Horowitch, J. The Elite College Students Who Can't Read Books. The Atlantic, October 1, 2024.

Engel, S. (2018). The Hungry Mind. The Origins of Curiosity in Childhood. Harvard University Press.

Dweck, C. (2007) Mindset: The New Psychology of Success (2nd Edition). Ballantine Books.

#4591. Garmin and Waze just teamed up on a clever new way to keep cyclists safer

Garmin and Waze are teaming up on an interesting new safety feature that could give cyclists a little extra protection when sharing the road with cars – by making cyclists themselves show up in Waze.

The new feature allows cyclists using a compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch to share their location through Garmin’s LiveTrack feature. That location can then appear in real time to nearby drivers using Waze, with cyclists displayed as moving icons on the road.

As someone who recently joined the Garmin family myself with a smartwatch for tracking my cycling, running, and other activities, this is exactly the type of feature I love seeing added to the platform.

I’ve long maintained that safety – or more accurately, the perception that cycling isn’t safe – is one of the biggest impediments to getting more people onto bikes.

That’s especially true in the US, where cyclists are often forced to share roads with cars instead of enjoying the kind of widespread separated cycling infrastructure found in many more bike-friendly countries. And when a cyclist and a multi-ton vehicle have to occupy the same space, making sure the driver knows that cyclist is there can make a big difference.

Of course, an icon on Waze isn’t going to magically make cycling safe. It won’t replace protected bike lanes, better road design, slower vehicle speeds, or attentive drivers.

But I can certainly imagine situations where it could help. Riding at night or in poor visibility, approaching a blind curve, or simply traveling on a narrow road where a driver might otherwise come upon a cyclist unexpectedly are all situations where an advance warning could be useful.

The feature is opt-in through Garmin Connect and activates when the cyclist starts an outdoor cycling activity. Garmin says location sharing is temporary and session-based, and that cyclists’ personal information isn’t displayed in Waze. Of course, anyone who uses a personal GPS device has already accepted that their location is shared with Big Tech in exchange for features they value, but at least we know that any personalized info stays within Garmin instead of proliferating even further.

This is cool but requires both a Garmin product and the Waze app. IMHO better to equip new cars and trucks with bicycle and pedestrian detection.

Garmin LiveTrack itself is free for users with compatible Garmin devices and previously allowed cyclists to share their live location, speed, route, and other information with friends and family. I’ve used it myself as a safety feature when venturing off-road and on longer solo journeys. The Waze integration essentially expands that safety net to nearby motorists.

There’s obviously one big limitation: You need to be riding with a compatible Garmin device, and the driver needs to be using Waze.

But with Waze claiming around 200 million users globally and Garmin being one of the biggest names in cycling computers and fitness watches, that’s not exactly a tiny Venn diagram.

Anything that gives drivers another chance to see cyclists before actually seeing them sounds like a win to me.

#4590. Sir Patrick Stewart Dies at 86 After Battle With Alzheimer's, Lewy Body Dementia

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Think of the home where you spent your childhood. You may still remember the room you slept in, the conversations you had there, the sound of someone calling you for dinner or the family and friends who came to visit on special occasions. Even years after leaving, that house may remain closely connected to your memories and sense of self.

Some people go beyond remembering their childhood homes and decide to buy them. But can recovering a childhood home also bring back the life once lived there?

Below, I explore that question through the experiences of three people who did exactly that. What made them want to reclaim these properties, and what did they discover when they returned? Their stories invite us to consider what it means to return to a place that remains so much a part of who we are.

Eddie Dilleen is one of Australia’s largest residential landlords; he owns more than 200 properties. But there was one property he could not buy. For more than 12 years, he waited for his childhood home to go on the market.

As he has written, ‘You can set reminders and stuff like that, but when I was on my phone messing around, I would randomly check it literally every one or two weeks for the past 12 years.’ When the house finally came on the market, he said, ‘I just bought it sight unseen.’ The price was just under $1 million. The house had been sold 25 years earlier for $97,000 following his parents’ divorce.

Eddie’s childhood home remained important to him throughout his adult life, even after he achieved financial success. His constant checking on it suggests an enduring emotional attachment to a place associated with loss and family separation. His decision to purchase the house without viewing it indicates a desperation to reclaim something he felt he had lost.

His experience also may be understood in the context of cognitive immobility, which can occur when an individual is unable to stay put in an intended place due to the absence or presence of certain restrictions or circumstances beyond their control, which may originate in their present or desired location, inside themselves, or in the external world.

Circumstances beyond Dilleen’s control made him leave his childhood home but some part of him remained in it.

Jenaca Rogers lived with her grandma but was also raised from infancy by her family friends, Pat and Jerry. Their house held many of her childhood memories, from family celebrations to everyday moments spent with her grandparents. When Pat and Jerry died, the house was sold following probate proceedings. As Jenaca recalled, ‘We were all heartbroken. Your whole life you hope for something and then it’s just taken away’.

Years later, in 2025, Jenaca unexpectedly discovered that the house was for sale, and called the estate agent. When he failed to answer, she said, ‘I just started crying because I was like, I’m not going to get it’.

She then found the agent’s mobile number online. She recalls, ‘I called him and he got us out there, and I cried in the driveway, I cried touring the house’. During the visit, she discovered her toy car in the backyard shed, which overwhelmed her further. She eventually bought the house and surprised her grandma, Connie, with a viewing. It was a homecoming for them both.

Buying the house brought Jenaca peace and comfort, but it did not erase her grief. Her experience suggests that reclaiming a meaningful place may help us feel emotionally connected with loved ones who have died but does not necessarily help with the loss.

Moving from Bogotá to Miami brought Colombian singer-songwriter Andrés Cepeda new opportunities and challenges, but he left behind something deeply personal. After years of searching for something he felt he had lost in Bogotá, he was able to recover it. Cepeda bought his childhood home.

After returning to the house, Cepeda said, 'I returned to the house, the street, the garden. Everything was just as I remembered. And yet nothing was the same. My parents were gone. My childhood was gone. Time itself had left.'

Cepeda may have experienced a sense of metaphorical homelessness, the idea that those who experience cognitive immobility may find out after returning home that ‘…no home is truly a home; even the previous home – the ancestral home – has lost its distinguishing features and allure’. Although Cepeda had recovered the property, his childhood experiences could not be recreated: 'I went on a personal tour of my life. The parks, the schools, the cafés, the houses of my friends, the places where my heart broke. All of it started turning into music.'

He wrote the song ‘Bogotá’ to express his feelings about his childhood city and family. As he describes it, ‘It captures the eerie, bittersweet feeling of returning to a place that once defined you – only to realise you miss not the place, but the person you were there’. Cepeda recovered his childhood home but could not recover his childhood. However, he could use his music to acknowledge what cannot be recovered.

Of the three stages of cognitive immobility, his music could have helped him enter the third stage, stabilisation, in which people ‘...tend to aim to retain values and pursue goals to help them with the loss, alleviating the sense of entrapment’.

Our childhood home can remain important long after we have left it. It is a reminder of the people we knew, our relationships and the experiences we had. If your childhood home has been lost through the breakup of your family, bereavement or some other circumstance beyond your control, recovering it may become a deeply personal goal.

The experiences of Dilleen, Rogers and Cepeda show that buying a childhood home can be a chance to reconnect with a familiar place, but it does not mean returning to the life once lived there. The building may remain but the people in it, the relationships, the life that existed there will have changed. We can return to a place without recovering the past and move forward without leaving its memories behind.

#4586. The new BMW i3 just proved how efficient an EV can be after a nearly 3,700-mile road trip

Who says long EV road trips mean hours at charging stations? BMW drove the new i3 for over 3 days, covering nearly 3,700 miles, and it took less than 3 hours of charging.

BMW put the i3 to the ultimate test of efficiency, charging speed, and long-distance EV capability on a nearly 3,700-mile Pan-European journey.

The Paneurpeana, as it’s called, is considered the benchmark for range and charging speed. The route begins at the North Cape in Norway, the northernmost point of continental Europe you can reach by car, and ends in Tarifa, Spain, the southernmost point of mainland Europe.

BMW drove the new i3 50 xDrive for a total of 3,658 miles (5,886.7 km) across eight countries and spent just 2 hours, 45 minutes, and 54 seconds charging at an average of 275 kW.

The performance beat the previous record by more than seven hours, according to Mike Reichelt, head of BMW’s Neue Klasse

BMW said the charging points were not predetermined and that it had to account for external factors such as weather and traffic jams.

The new i3 was impressively efficient during the trip, consuming an average of just 12.5 kWh per 100 km, beating its official WLTP combined energy consumption of 18-13.4 kWh/100 km.

BMW said the trip took 3 days, 2 hours, and 41 minutes, with an average speed of 79.7 km/h, and that the i3 was charged exclusively at public charging points across national charging networks.

The vehicle was driven at all times by a single driver and was not modified in any way, in terms of hardware or software, from the standard i3 available for purchase.

BMW’s new i3 uses a 108.7 kWh battery and Gen6 eDrive system that provides a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).

With a drag coefficient of just 0.21, the new i3 is the most aerodynamically efficient BMW vehicle to date.

In the US, BMW said the new 2027 i3 50 xDrive will offer an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 468 miles.

With an 800V architecture, the electric sedan can add nearly 262 miles (423 km) of range (WLTP) in about 10 minutes at DC fast-charging speeds up to 400 kW. In the US, the i3 has a built-in NACS port.

Very reasonable. I've been with NK iX3 from Spain to Estonia and the experience is real - low consumption, great comfort and really fast charging. And there are more and more high speed chargers every month.

Like the new iX3, the i3 features BMW’s Neue Klasse interior design. The setup consists of BMW’s massive 43″ Panoramic Vision display that spans the base of the windshield and a 17.9″ floating central infotainment display.

The new BMW i3 50 xDrive is on sale in Germany starting at €65,900 with a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).

In the US, the 2027 BMW i3 50 xDrive and 2027 iX3 50 xDrive are available to order, both starting at $61,500.

#4584. 4 Ways Parents Can Support Teen Online Safety and Well-Being

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

I recently asked 30 young people what they wished their parents understood about their online lives. One young person’s story shows how easily parents can overlook online risks.

Blake (not their real name) was in fifth grade when an adult approached them on Amino, a now-defunct social media platform. Their conversation quickly evolved into what Blake thought of as a romantic relationship.

Looking back, Blake told me, “It was obviously incredibly unsafe,” and added, “I wish someone had found out about it earlier on.”

Blake never told their parents because they believed that they were “doing something wrong.” While Blake’s parents monitored their YouTube watch history, Blake now wishes their parents had engaged in more open conversations about their online life and set “more (tech) restrictions early on.” Contrary to what many parents might think, Blake didn’t want to be left alone. They wanted their parents to ask them about their online life and set clearer boundaries, making it easier to ask for help.

In my conversations, young people shared four practical tips for talking with teens about their online lives and supporting their online safety and well-being.

Due to fear of punishment or disapproval, young people often hide their online lives from parents. This secrecy is driven by the same reason teens don’t share that they were offered a drink at a party. They’re afraid it will get them in trouble, or they'll be cut off from their friends.

One young LGBTQ+ woman, for example, said that her very religious dad monitored her social media feeds and told her to delete any post he disagreed with. He did the same to her adult siblings. This didn’t stop her from posting. Instead, she learned how to moderate what he could see.

Other young people described what happened when parents responded with curiosity rather than judgment. When one young woman’s mom found her secret Twitter account, she expected to be grounded “for a million years.” Instead, her mom calmly asked who she was talking to. The young woman said that her mom’s response made room for conversation and connection.

When teens feel like they have to hide their online lives, they’re less likely to come to their parents when something goes wrong. Young people told us that when parents act as digital coaches, staying calm and walking them through difficult situations, they build online safety skills, and their relationships with their parents grow stronger. Being a coach doesn’t mean ignoring risks or abandoning rules. It means listening, understanding what happened, and helping your teen work through difficult situations.

Existing research and our conversations with young people both point to the importance of talking with teens about their online lives. Similar to talking to teens about other sensitive topics like drinking and sex, it’s more effective to have the conversation before it's relevant. Think of it less like a “Sit down; we have to talk” lecture and more like a series of low-pressure chats.

There are many good conversation guides for parents, including from Internet Matters, Common Sense Media, and the Spark and Stitch Institute. By using nonjudgmental, open-ended questions such as “What’s something you’ve enjoyed online lately?” or “How do you feel about your school’s AI policy?” parents can show curiosity without making teens defensive. Current events, like the recent Meta settlement, can also serve as a springboard for conversation.

It can help to keep expectations for these conversations low. Even the best-timed and well-intentioned conversations are likely to be met with eye rolls by teens. That’s OK. As teen psychologist and author Lisa Damour explains, “Your (kid) may roll her eyes, but do it anyway. (Kids) can listen and roll their eyes at the same time.” Her podcast episode, “Untangling All Things Digital for Parents,” is worth a listen.

As a parent, I was surprised and heartened to learn that not all tech rules feel restrictive to teens. Several were even grateful for them. One teen boy I spoke with said, “[My parents] make me leave my phone downstairs … I think that's a good idea because I don't wanna be using my phone. I'm trying to sleep because I have to wake up really early.”

Young people told us that their parents’ tech use shaped their own, for better and worse. One young adult said a lack of healthy boundaries at home left “no real role model to follow.” Another said her mother now tells her to ask an AI chatbot before coming to her for advice.

Modeling healthy habits is one of the most powerful tools parents have. When parents spend a lot of time on digital media, their teens tend to do so as well. Moreover, teens who feel like their parents are more focused on their devices than on them report higher depression. Parents can strengthen their relationship and teach healthy tech habits at the same time by holding themselves to the same standards that they set for their teen. This might look like modeling the importance of sleep by agreeing that everyone in the house, including parents, keeps phones out of the bedroom after 10 p.m.

You don’t need to model perfection. You can acknowledge when you get distracted or struggle to maintain a boundary. Saying, “I’ve been checking my phone too much during dinner, so I’m going to leave it in the other room,” makes your own effort visible. Shared expectations show that healthy tech habits are a family responsibility, not just something parents impose on teens.

Parents are being asked to make high-stakes decisions about fast-changing technology, often without shared norms or practical support. They shouldn’t have to carry this burden alone, but tech companies and federal regulatory agencies aren’t adequately stepping up.

Fortunately, you don’t need to be a tech expert to listen to teens, set thoughtful boundaries, and make it easier for your teen to ask for help. What helps teens most is a strong, trusting relationship with their parents. Research backs this up: A warm parent-child relationship, alongside clear boundaries, predicts safer internet use among teens. Over time, a compassionate and collaborative approach can help teens navigate technology skillfully, with less secrecy and power struggles and more mutual respect.

Emma Bruehlman-Senecal, Ph.D., is a social psychologist and Principal Researcher at Hopelab, where she partners with young people to design tools that advance youth mental health and well-being.

#4581. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4579. The Meaning and Value of Stress

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

For the last 60 years or so, we've been warned about stress and told to do everything we can to avoid it.

We've been taught how to meditate our way out of stress, down-regulate from it, "hack our cortisol," reduce our adrenaline, manage our vagus nerve, calm ourselves, numb ourselves, distract ourselves, and halt our stress responses in as many ways as we can.

We've also been taught to view many of the difficulties in our lives as always-negative exterior forces, or stressors, that act upon us without our knowledge or permission. Stress has been presented to us as a dangerously unwanted thing with no value whatsoever.

Thankfully, newer research into stressors and our stress response has found the opposite to be true.

In part 1 of this series, I focused on the weasel word of stress, because our stress response is an emotional response. In my work, Dynamic Emotional Integration, I help people understand the emotions that form the foundation of our stress response. We learn how to name these emotions with precision and work directly with them to access the essential intelligence they contribute to us.

Three of the main emotions I see in our stress response are: anxiety (the emotion of motivation and task completion), anger (which helps us identify and uphold what we value), and panic (which steps forward when our lives are in danger).

Each of these emotions helps us meet stressors with intelligence and focus. When we know which emotions are supporting us, and we know how to work with those emotions (instead of against them), stressful situations can teach us who we are, what's important to us, and how we can meet life's challenges with focus, skills, and resilience.

But if we don't know how to identify or work with our emotions, we may feel overwhelmed as our bodies increase our activation to help us meet the necessary stressors we face. We may also learn two unhelpful lessons:

If we believe that stressors are foreign and that our emotions are problems, we'll create unnecessary suffering, not just in response to the stressors but because our skills are missing in action.

Psychological researcher Kelly McGonigal has been focusing on stress for many years, and in her 2016 book, The Upside of Stress: Why Stress Is Good for You, and How to Get Good at It, she shares information from decades of stress research. Her book is full of surprising facts that turn our understanding of stress on its ear. For instance:

If I told you that the price of tiger chow has gone up by 40 percent, you might have little to no reaction (assuming you aren't a tiger keeper). This is a big price increase, but because it has no meaning to you and does not impact any part of your life, your stress response will be quiet—as it should be; there's nothing for you to do about this, and your emotions don't need to be involved.

But if I told you that your share of the cost for your child's monthly doctor's visits has gone up by 40 percent, it's likely that your stress response would engage. Your emotions, most notably anxiety and anger, might intensify to bring you the energy and focus you need to work the problem. Your stress response would help you know that this situation is important, that it's worth your time and focus, and that you need its increased energy to help you make new plans to support your child's well-being.

Sadly, most stress management approaches would have you try to calm yourself or suppress your emotions (or merely observe them), as if the activation you feel is a problem in and of itself. But this old, tired idea is not only wrong; it's counterproductive, because the strength of your stress response is a key to your success and even mastery of the situation.

Of all the surprising things in stress research, this may be the most delightful: The strength of your stress response—your emotional intensity, your hyper-focus, your "nerves"—is directly connected to your ability to thrive. And this continues to be true even when you're well-acquainted with a stressor and no longer see it as surprising or shocking.

Researchers studied new and seasoned skydivers, certain that they would see a reduced stress response (reduced cortisol, adrenaline, and heart rate, less "stress") as the skydivers became accustomed to throwing themselves out of planes. Strangely, there wasn't any reduction in the markers of stress in the seasoned skydivers; in fact, the most skilled skydivers continued to exhibit very high stress responses, often higher than people jumping out of planes for the first time.

What they did find was that the seasoned skydivers had reframed their stress responses as excitement, readiness, stimulation, and even zest for life. This reframing helped them treat their activation as a necessary and fun part of skydiving, even though they might have experienced the exact same stress response as overwhelming the first time they leapt out of a plane.

This seemingly paradoxical relationship holds true for other high-performers such as athletes, surgeons, artists, actors, and musicians. A higher stress response does not predict failure; it is intimately connected to skill and mastery.

So, the key is not to avoid stressors or your stress response, and it's not to become an endlessly chilled-out and calm person.

The key to developing your resilience alongside your skills is to learn how to reframe your natural responses to stressors and welcome the stimulation, focus, and preparedness they provide.

In Part 3: How to reframe your stress response

McGonigal, K. (2016). The Upside of Stress: Why Stress Is Good for You, and How to Get Good at It. New York, NY: Avery.

#4578. BYD and Geely approached FIA about a 12th F1 team, says Ben Sulayem

BYD and Geely have both approached the FIA about entering Formula 1, the sport’s governing body confirmed. FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem named the two Chinese automakers while speaking at the New Economy Forum in Madrid, as first reported by Grande Prêmio.

But there’s no open process for a 12th team, and neither company has a deal. The FIA is also pushing F1 toward the kind of engine an EV maker has the least reason to build.

“One of them was BYD and another was Geely,” Ben Sulayem said of the manufacturers that have reached out about joining the grid.

He said he suggested that BYD buy an existing team instead of starting a new one. BYD wasn’t interested in that route. It wants its own team, so Ben Sulayem told the company to come back with a “serious proposal” that shows the project can work.

He also made it clear that Chinese manufacturers won’t get special treatment. Any bid would go through the same process as other prospective entrants, and the rules won’t be rewritten to suit them. Right now, there’s no expansion process at all: the FIA isn’t actively looking for a 12th team.

Still, Ben Sulayem repeated that he’d like F1’s next newcomer to come from China, pointing to the country’s EV technology and the Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai.

This isn’t new for BYD. Back in March, we reported that BYD was exploring a Formula 1 entry, either by buying a team or building one from scratch.

In April, executive vice president Stella Li said BYD had met F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali in Shanghai and that an entry was “something we’re discussing.” By July, the tone had cooled. Li said “the dream is always there, but we don’t have a concrete agenda,” and special advisor Alfredo Altavilla set a clear condition: “We will never participate in Formula 1 just to put a sticker on the side of a car.”

Altavilla said BYD would only consider F1 to the extent its technology can serve the sport.

Geely is the new name here. The group sold 3.02 million vehicles last year and owns Volvo, Polestar, and Lotus, a brand with decades of F1 history. It’s also heading into Canada next year as Chinese automakers push hard into new markets.

The last newcomer, Cadillac, took a long road. The FIA opened an expression-of-interest process in 2023, and GM’s team only joined the grid as the 11th team this season, running Ferrari power until its own power unit arrives. Audi got in the other way, by taking over Sauber.

Here’s where it gets awkward for an EV maker. The 2026 F1 power units split output roughly 50/50 between the combustion engine and electric power, with the MGU-K jumping to 350 kW.

The FIA is already walking that back. In June, it agreed to shift the split to 60-40 in favor of combustion for 2027 and 2028. And Ben Sulayem has been pushing for V8 engines running on sustainable fuel with “minor electrification” for the next rules cycle, starting in 2031 at the latest, possibly 2030. Domenicali says F1 should have a package ready to discuss by the end of this year.

So the FIA president wants a Chinese EV maker on the grid, while pushing a rulebook that makes their main strength less relevant.

We like the idea of BYD or Geely in F1. Chinese automakers have the money and the engineers, and they badly need brand prestige outside China. BYD in particular has been on a performance push with Yangwang, and F1 would be the loudest possible way to tell Europe it’s not just a cheap car brand.

they look for visibility/recognition on the world stage, regardless EVs. And in some (primitive) markets they market themselves as hybrids automakers, not as EV automakers.

They will make a hybrid power unit (which they already make anyway) to comply with the backward F1 regulations.

But Ben Sulayem’s comments don’t move things much. There’s no entry process, BYD has already turned down his main suggestion, and Geely’s interest is a name dropped at a conference, not a bid.

A Chinese would likely be good for F1 as well. Motorsports are on the rise in China, and that would be the cherry on top in helping popularize the sport in the world’s largest market.

The bigger issue is the engine. Altavilla was clear that BYD isn’t interested in slapping a logo on a car. It wants F1 to showcase its technology, and BYD’s technology is batteries and electric drive. The FIA’s V8 push goes the other way. It’s hard to sell an EV giant on a sport that’s reducing the electric part of the powertrain.

#4576. Watch BYD’s robotic charging arm plug itself in and charge EVs in 5 minutes [Video]

BYD’s Flash Charging tech can charge an EV in as little as five minutes. Now, BYD is taking things a step further with integrated solar power and a robotic arm that plugs itself in. See how it all works in action.

After unveiling the Yangwang Altior in the UAE on Monday, its new ultra-luxury flagship electric sedan, BYD showcased its latest breakthrough technology.

The Chinese automaker launched a new integrated charging system in the Abu Dhabi desert that brings BYD’s “Three Green Dreams” to life.

In 2006, BYD president and CEO Wang Chuanfu revealed his vision of “Three Green Dreams,” including harnessing solar power to generate renewable energy, storing that energy in batteries, and replacing gas-powered vehicles with electric ones that run on clean energy.

The new charging system is the “world’s first,” according to BYD, to integrate solar power generation, energy storage, Flash Charging, and robotic charging together in one solution.

BYD’s Flash Charging tech enables a vehicle’s battery to charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, essentially the same time it takes to fill up at a gas station. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

The new robotic charging arm automatically locates the vehicle’s charging port, opens its cover, plugs in, and then removes it once the session is over.

By combining robotic charging with its Automated Valet Parking, BYD said the new tech goes beyond automated driving and parking to the charging process itself.

Once the vehicle is parked, the robotic charging arm automatically takes over and connects it to Flash Charging without the driver even touching the cable.

A post shared by Michael Martinez (@mmichael_martinez)

Michaël Martinez, head of marketing at BYD France, posted a video (shown above) showcasing the new charging tech in action.

The integrated solution is built around BYD’s Solar-Storage-Charging (SSC) system, fusing solar energy generation, battery storage, and its 5-minute Flash Charging tech. Together, the setup captures energy from the sun, stores it, and distributes it as needed.

If they could tie this into a smart summon type of capability, where the vehicle communicates with the charger and moves the vehicle into the proper location for charging and then moves to a parking spot once charging is complete. Rental car fleets would benefit and so would those in shopping centers. There are so many possibilities and this looks far more mature that the old snake charging Tesla demoed.

BYD has over 16 years of experience in the solar industry with a portfolio that includes solar cells, modules, and systems.

Its solar division, BYD Solar, does business in over 100 countries and regions. By using solar power, BYD said, the SCC system can operate independently off-the-grid.

The new technology is part of BYD’s wider Flash Charging rollout. By the end of 2027, the company plans to deploy 6,000 Flash Charging stations globally.

#4575. Why Certain Pop Songs Trigger Inexplicable Emotion

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Recently, I was scrolling through the Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1980. I was 14 years old that year, making it the absolute peak of my "musical reminiscence bump," the developmental window when our brains permanently wire the music of our youth to our deepest emotions.

While perusing the list, I realized there's one song that always stops me dead in my tracks and hits surprisingly hard whenever it catches me off guard in a random place, like a supermarket checkout line. That song is Elton John's "Little Jeannie."

Lyrically, this song doesn't say anything profoundly moving until near the end. And the refrain "I want you to be my acrobat, I want you to be my lover" always seems like a throwaway line. On paper, the song could easily be categorized as a seriously schmaltzy, mid-tempo early '80s pop song.

Nevertheless, every time I hear the opening percussion and cascading drum intro, I get verklempt. During the 20-second, lyric-free introduction that might sound like "Muzak-y" elevator music to some, my emotions swell and I'm filled with a deep sense of, for lack of a better word, "wistfulness" that doesn't make sense to me logically.

Curious if I was alone in having such a poignant response to a somewhat cheesy pop song, I looked at the YouTube comments to see if other listeners echoed my sentiment.

Notably, for many of the "Little Jeannie" versions on YouTube, all of which are sung in English by Elton John, the comment sections are dominated by foreign-language responses (lots of Portuguese!). According to Google Translate, these comments convey that even among non-English speakers or ESL listeners, "Little Jeannie" hits hard in bittersweet ways that seem to catch people off guard.

While sifting through various comments, I found two that elucidate the inexplicable power of "Little Jeannie" to stir emotions:

Why does a song that isn't inherently sad make someone cry? And how can a listener feel nostalgia for an era they didn't live through? As it turns out, the answers lie in a fascinating intersection of behavioral psychology, imagination, and neuroscience.

A new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) on November 16, 2026, investigated the sociocultural dimensions of music-evoked memories. The researchers played 30-second clips of billboard-topping hits to 223 college students, utilizing songs from their own teenage years (the 2010s) and their parents' teenage years (the 1980s and 1990s).

Using natural language processing to analyze the memories these songs evoked, the researchers found that certain songs reliably generated strikingly similar memory scenarios among strangers from comparable backgrounds, driven by culturally learned "scripts."

To find out where that emotion was coming from, the researchers stripped away the music and gave a separate group of participants just a song's lyrics to read. Without music accompanying the words to a song, the shared sociocultural dimensions of people's autobiographical memories and associations diminished.

Based on this observation, the researchers concluded that the lyrics alone don't drive our intense reactions to pop music. Instead, the emotional scripts are embedded in the musical sound and genre itself.

When a YouTube commenter notes that "Little Jeannie" isn't a sad song but makes their eyes well up with tears, it isn't necessarily the lyrics driving that reaction. It's the specific acoustic architecture created by an old Fender Rhodes electric piano, alto saxophone, and flugelhorn, all wrapped in layered vocal harmonies. This unique musical alchemy tugs directly at the heartstrings, completely bypassing the analytical mind where words reside.

How does neuroscience explain the enigma of a young listener feeling "ridiculously melancholic" when hearing a song released decades before they were born?

One possible explanation: While we experience a primary surge of memory attachment for the music of our own adolescence, we also develop a secondary attachment to the music of our parents and caregivers from earlier generations. As the authors explain in their recent PNAS paper:

"Interestingly, however, music-evoked autobiographical memories (MEAMs) are characterized by a potentially unique phenomenon known as 'cascading reminiscence bumps,' in which they exhibit a secondary reminiscence bump associated with music that was popular before listeners were born."

As children, we're often captive audiences in the backseat of a car or the family living room. Long before music was siloed into individual earbuds via streaming apps, "hard copy" formats like vinyl records, CDs, and mixtapes filled these shared spaces. Played aloud on common speakers, we passively absorbed our parents' adolescent soundtracks by osmosis.

Yet, even as modern listening habits shift toward isolated headphones, this intergenerational phenomenon persists. This new (2026) study suggests that these cultural "scripts" are so deeply wired into us that even if a younger participant had never heard a specific older song before, their brain can use the song's genre to automatically retrieve a feeling that fits the cultural vibe.

Because these acoustic architectures activate shared neural representations, the emotional script transcends both the generation and the delivery method.

Another recent study by Princeton's Elizabeth Margulis and colleagues, published in Nature Communications on August 18, 2026, used fMRI to explore the neural representations of imagined narratives that participants conjured up while listening to unfamiliar music.

During the experiment, researchers scanned people's brains while they listened to completely instrumental tracks. The scans revealed that across different test subjects, the music produced highly organized, shared patterns in the brain's default mode network (DMN). As the authors explain:

"This work demonstrates that music elicits detectable, modality-general representations, a kind of higher-order 'meaning', integrating both narrative imagery and its associated emotional profile, specific to particular excerpts."

Interestingly, Margulis's team found that the DMN doesn't need semantic language to engage in profound meaning-making. This helps to explain why it's almost impossible to pinpoint why certain music evokes shared imagined narratives; these emotions bubble up outside the realm of words (i.e., lexical semantics).

According to the latest 2026 research, music has the power to tap into a cultural frequency that bypasses our critical minds, reminding us that oftentimes, profound meaning is found in things we feel deeply but can't articulate.

Cara Turnbull, Benjamin M. Kubit, Kelly Jakubowski, Elizabeth H. Margulis. Music Illuminates Sociocultural Dimensions of Autobiographical Memory. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (First published: November 16, 2026) doi:10.1073/pnas.2536885123

Elizabeth Margulis, Uri Hasson, Itamar Jalon, Jamal Williams, Grace Simmons, Karen Electra Christianson, Cara Turnbull. Music Evokes Shared Neural Representations of Imagined Narratives Across Sensory Modalities. Nature Communications (First published: August 18, 2026) doi:10.1038/s41467-026-76452-0

Kelly Jakubowski, Tuomas Eerola, Barbara Tillmann, Fabien Perrin, Lizette Heine. A Cross-Sectional Study of Reminiscence Bumps for Music-Related Memories in Adulthood. Music & Science (First published: October 23, 2020) doi:10.1177/2059204320965058

#4574. 6 Best Heart Rate Monitors, Tested by Our Fitness Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Knowledge is power when it comes to performance, these picks help you get it.

TRAINING WITHOUT TRACKING is like shooting a basketball without knowing where the hoop is, especially if you have an ultimate goal like running a marathon or increasing your VO2 max. Many people reach a point in their fitness journey where they hit a plateau, and more often than not, that flatline results from not having the right information. So if you're hitting the gym on a regular basis and putting in the work, it can be important to make sure that you are getting all the relevant health insights to make sure you're using your time efficiently.

A few of the most important insights are heart rate variability (HRV), which describes the difference in time between the beats of your heart, and resting heart rate (RHR), which is the number of times your heart pumps while you are awake, relaxed and not moving. Heart rate monitors (HRMs) are the best way to get this data.

Understanding your HRV can help you make better workout choices and understand when it's time to recover. Generally speaking, your resting heart rate will become lower as your fitness level increases, indicating more efficient heart function and improved cardiovascular fitness. “Over time (and months of tracking your resting heart rate), you'll notice patterns. Maybe your RHR spikes every weekend, in part because you're out late Saturday nights. Or it's lower on Mondays, because you go to bed earlier on Sundays," says MH Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. "All of this data can help you make smart lifestyle tweaks that aid your overall wellness — and set you up to move, look, and feel your best and most alert, whether you're in the gym or at the office.”

With the holidays coming up fast, it’s a good time to add a heart rate monitor to your wish list. It can help you start your New Year’s training goals on a data-driven note, and allow you to track your progress over time.

Ready to take your training to the next level? Read on to find the best heart rate monitors for you and what to consider when looking for a HRM.

We've been raving about Whoop for years, and it's still one of our favorite fitness trackers simply because it collects so much useful data. This stylish and understated device uses PPG sensors to continuously check your heart rate, and can use the data it captures to figure out when your deepest sleep is happening.

Every day it delivers a recovery percentage and suggests the level of activity you should aim for, whether that a five-mile run or a rest day. In the past, the brand stuck with a simple black band, but these days there are more color and style options for anyone wanting to elevate the look of their HRM.

I personally am a fan of the ability to check my insights when I want, without a distractingly bright screen that pulls my attention.

While products like the Whoop band and the Oura Ring are relatively new on the scene, Garmin has been making wearable fitness trackers for a long time now. This heart rate monitor transmits real-time heart rate data over ANT+ connectivity and Bluetooth, giving you the immediate feedback you need to take your performance to the next level.

This Garmin comes with a rechargeable battery with a seriously long life (two months). It charges easily using the provided 4-pin charging cable, similar to the ones that come with their watches.

We were also impressed with how comfortable this strap is to wear, made out of a lightweight nylon weave. For placement, you want to put the sensor in the middle of your ribcage against your skin, not over your clothes, so that it can get the best readings. Once you are done with your run, you will be able to connect it to your smartphone or Garmin watch via Bluetooth, and then pull up your stats from the menu option.

Because this Garmin has Bluetooth, it is also able to connect pretty simply to cardio machines at your gym like treadmills if you want to track your workouts there. If you are a Garmin fan, and want even more functionality and access to the Garmin Connect app, you may want to spring for the Garmin HRM Pro model (about $60 more).

Read More: Best Fitness Trackers, Tested by Us

This is a subtle and sleek way to monitor your heart rate throughout the day. Most people aren't going to wear a ring like this while lifting weights, which is why we love the Oura Ring to track those important metrics during the 23 hours of the day that you're not at the gym. What's most impressive about the Oura Ring is its small size, and how one small ring can monitor your sleep, steps, and heart rate.

This ring gives you all the information you need to make improvements in your daily health and well-being. For those looking to try a smart ring for the first time, it doesn't get better than Oura, which is why it took the top spot in our best smart rings testing and this head-to-head piece against the Samsung Galaxy Ring.

Read More: The Oura Ring Vs. the Galaxy Ring

The Apple Watch is by far one of the most popular smartwatches on the market, and like the Samsung Galaxy Watch 8, it also tracks quite a lot of data, including heart rate. Although not as accurate as the chest bands, the Apple Watch 12 gets the job done well enough for the casual fitness goer.

In addition to heart rate, it also features an SpO2 sensor to monitor blood oxygen level readings, an ECG to test for atrial fibrillation, fitness tracking, sleep monitoring, and all the run-of-the-mill smartwatch features. Our editors have already spent some time with this latest release, and it's fair to say we're suitably impressed.

The Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 is essentially a wearable personal trainer and advisor powered by AI. With built-in pace coaching and a heart rate monitor, you can add and customize your workouts for maximum efficiency, helping you reach your fitness goals in no time. It connects to your smartphone so you can easily take calls, receive texts, or pull up directions with the flick of your wrist.

The newer design is certainly better looking than previous editions. The integrated Run Coach also impressed some of our editors, guiding those who require additional motivation.

That being said, despite the fact that the Galaxy Watch 8 supports iOS and iPhone users through its companion app, those users might be better over going for the Apple Watch Ultra 3 for the additional integrations. The heart rate measurements and sleep tracking is where this device really shines, which is perfect for those looking for a new HRM.

Read more: Best Smartwatches, Tested By Us

While it’s not the latest version, the Pixel Watch 4 from Google is packed with useful features beginners will appreciate. (The Pixel Watch 5 is the newest iteration, but significantly more expensive.) One of our favorites is Active Zone Minutes, which uses your resting heart rate to gauge exercise effort and give you a buzz when it's time to step up the intensity so you can make the most of your workouts. It monitors activity, sleep, and nightly blood oxygen levels, tracking your trends over time to see important changes in your overall health.

This is a great pick for anyone looking to get great health insights from a wrist piece, who also would like a subtly stylish look. Since Google now owns Fitbit, this watch features some of that great Fitbit technology, which means there are a lot of great integrations if you have a Google account. But because of this, the pairing with iOS devices is not optimal. Something to take into consideration if you're an Apple user.

Google also knows how to make app experiences easy on new users, including older users without a lot of time with technology.

The biggest determination you need to make before purchasing is what your primary goal is for the heart rate monitor. Competitive triathletes may want to splurge on a top-shelf device that wraps around your chest for the most accurate data. Whereas beginners or more casual users might opt for a more modest option they can wear throughout the day (like a general fitness tracker) for daily health insights. Perhaps you spend a lot of time on the golf course and want to know how your heart handles hours of walking combined with the stress of trying to make par. Of course, you may be one of those high-performing individuals who uses both.

Beyond finding a device that fits your performance needs, you also need one that fits well on your body. This depends on whether you choose a chest strap, a wristband, or a smart ring. In most cases, the sensors need to be secured tightly against your body to get accurate readings. Take accurate body measurements before ordering offline, and be prepared to return for a different size if you need to (especially with something like a chest strap). If you are looking into smart rings, many of the options, like the Oura Ring we list, will ship out sizing kits for a small fee to get the correct fit.

Great data is useless if you don’t have an easy means of getting it. For devices without screens, make sure you check which smartphones and apps they are compatible with. They will usually connect with your personal devices through Bluetooth. For devices with screens, check images of the user interface to make sure you’ll enjoy it. Of course, the devices we are suggesting here with screens will display all the important information you’ll want. But some may have better compatibility with iOS or Android, which you’ll want to consider.

With the exception of the Apple Watches (Ultra 3 and Series 11) and the Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 (two heart rate monitors that are equal parts smartwatch), the heart rate monitors we tested are all designed to run for days (even weeks) on a single charge. We love a heart rate monitor that needs minimal charging, and we also love one that lasts a long time in non-connected mode. Two heart rate monitors that surprised us when testing battery life include the Garmin HRM-Dual (3.5 years if used for one hour a day) and the Oura Ring (7 days while on).

Being the Fitness and Commerce Editor at Men's Health, it's my job to evaluate the latest and greatest training gear. This includes fitness trackers, and throughout the year, I get the latest designs from the best brands, both new and old. I am also a certified trainer, and my personal training includes a wide range of exercises, from boxing to lifting to sprint work. But this story was a collective effort by several editors, who were enlisted to try different models and types of trackers based on their preferences.

We tested each tracker for at least two weeks and put it through a range of exercise scenarios, from treadmill sprints to weighted pull-ups to deadlifts. My fellow testers included certified trainers who also happen to be editors at Men's Health, like Samuel. For devices that have been around for several updates, we've used most of them since they hit the market. Our tested selection didn't focus on chasing trends. Instead, our picks of the best fitness trackers provide great value and performance at reasonable price points for the data they provide.

#4573. Tesla Cybertruck had its best month in over a year. It’s still going away

New EV prices edged up in October, but buyers still paid less than they did a year ago. The average transaction price for a new EV in the US was $56,220, up 1% from September and down 2.7% from October 2025, according to Kelley Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand.

Across all new vehicles, the average hit a record $51,109, up 1.3% from September and 2.1% year over year, even as prices rose more slowly than they typically do in October.

EV incentives barely budged from September’s revised 11.2% of the average transaction price to 11.3% in October. That’s up from 10.3% a year earlier and well above October’s industrywide average of 6.8%.

Tesla’s average selling price fell from September to $54,194, but it was still up 1.2% year over year. The Cybertruck helped push that average higher. Cox Automotive estimates Tesla sold 1,914 Cybertrucks in October, its best month in more than a year, at an average price of $92,380.

The sad thing is that there likely is a market for an affordable electric pickup truck in the U.S. to compete with Ford’s F150 and others. The Ford Fathom may be the best fit for that market, now.

That sales bump comes as Tesla prepares to end Cybertruck production at its Austin factory in mid-2027. Elon Musk said Tesla will dismantle the assembly line around June or July to make room for more Cybercab robotaxis.

#4572. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

#4571. Lucid CEO admits it ‘did not even know where cars were’ and lost orders

Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the company’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.

That’s a rough admission from a company sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles. And it’s a problem Tesla ran into, and fixed, back in 2018 at more than ten times Lucid’s current volume.

Napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter. He said that at the start of Q3, the company had orders where it “would take sometimes two weeks to deliver to the customer, and so we would lose the order.”

He said Lucid now has visibility on which cars are being built, where they’re shipped, where they’re stored, and when they can reach a customer. A new commercial team also now sells the cars it knows are available on the day a customer wants one.

Lucid built 3,228 more vehicles than it delivered in the first half of 2026, including 5,500 built but only 3,093 delivered in Q1. Its inventory hit $1.38 billion on the balance sheet at the end of June, which is why we reported earlier this year that Lucid had to adjust production after a bloated Q1 inventory.

So Lucid had thousands of cars on lots and in transit, and it was still losing buyers because it couldn’t match a car to an order fast enough.

In Q3, Lucid cut production to 2,954 vehicles and delivered 3,806, down 7% year over year. Finished goods inventory fell by almost 15% during the quarter, according to new CFO Alexander De Bock. Inventory stood at $1.22 billion on September 30.

Tesla learned this lesson the hard way during the Model 3 ramp.

By Q3 2018, Tesla was making roughly 4,000 Model 3s per week. That’s more cars every week than Lucid delivers in a full quarter today. Deliveries tripled or quadrupled in some markets, and the bottleneck moved from the factory to the trucks.

Elon Musk tweeted in September 2018 that Tesla had “gone from production hell to delivery logistics hell.” A week later, he said Tesla was facing an “extreme shortage of car carrier trailers” and had started building its own car carriers to keep cars moving. Tesla also launched door-to-door delivery and asked existing owners to help at delivery centers.

It didn’t stop there. In November 2018, with the federal tax credit about to be cut in half for Tesla buyers, Musk said Tesla had bought trucking companies and locked in contracts with major haulers. Tesla moved cars east by truck instead of rail to cut weeks off transit times.

Tesla delivered 83,500 vehicles in Q3 2018, including 55,840 Model 3s, a record at the time.

When Model 3 reached Europe in February 2019, the first ship docked at Zeebrugge in Belgium and Tesla immediately had trouble processing the cars at the port.

About a week after the first ship arrived, Tesla ended its contract with the company preparing Model 3s at the port and took over the work itself. The target was 3,000 cars per week coming through one port.

It worked. By March 2019, Tesla delivered more than 5,300 Model 3s in Norway alone, making it the best-selling car in the country by a wide margin. A car that’s sitting at a port or on a lot doesn’t make anyone money. Tesla treated delivery speed as a sales tool, not a back-office job.

We later learned from Musk himself that this “logistic hell” was almost the nail in Tesla’s coffin. The CEO said that Tesla was at the brink of bankruptcy at the time.

I like to think people were relatively patient with Tesla's growing pains when Model 3 was ramping up in 2018, largely because there weren't many alternatives for a sporty, relatively affordable EV.

But it's 2026. Buyers have plenty of options now, and the patience that early EV adopters once had for these kinds of mistakes is long gone.

This is one of the most embarrassing admissions we’ve heard on an earnings call, and credit to Napoli for saying it out loud. Most executives would have blamed “demand” and moved on.

But it explains a lot. Lucid’s problem has never been the cars. The Air and Gravity are excellent products. The problem has been everything around them: service, software, and now we learn, basic inventory tracking. When you’re spending about $273,000 for every car you deliver, losing a buyer because you can’t find their car two weeks after they ordered is brutal.

Tesla solved this at 4,000 Model 3s a week while fighting for its own survival. Lucid is moving fewer than 300 cars a week. This isn’t a hard problem at that scale. It’s a discipline problem, and Napoli is right to call it that.
